problem_context: Find indices of two numbers in an array that add up to target.
user_code_snippet: for i in range(n): for j in range(i+1, n): if nums[i]+nums[j]==target: return [i,j]
hint: Your O(n²) nested loop approach is correct but too slow for large inputs. For each element x, you only need to know if (target - x) exists somewhere. Think about a data structure that gives you O(1) lookup of previously seen values.

problem_context: Find indices of two numbers in an array that add up to target.
user_code_snippet: sort array with indices, use two pointers
hint: Sorting with two pointers finds the values but loses the original indices. You would need to store (value, original_index) pairs before sorting. A simpler path: a single-pass hashmap stores value→index directly without sorting.

problem_context: Find indices of two numbers in an array that add up to target.
user_code_snippet: seen = {}; for i,x in enumerate(nums): if target-x in seen: return [seen[target-x], i]; seen[x]=i
hint: Excellent approach. Your single-pass hashmap is optimal at O(n) time and O(n) space. One edge case to consider: what if the same element is used twice? Your map insertion after the lookup check handles this correctly.

problem_context: Find indices of two numbers in an array that add up to target.
hint: Start simple: for each number x in the array, the number you need is (target - x). The challenge is finding that complement quickly. What if you built a lookup table of all numbers you have seen so far as you iterate?

problem_context: Find indices of two numbers in an array that add up to target.
user_code_snippet: sort array, compare adjacent elements
hint: Adjacent elements after sorting rarely sum to target. Sorting also destroys original indices which you need in your answer. Restart without sorting: think about what you need to remember from previous elements while iterating once.

problem_context: Check if a bracket string is valid: brackets must close in correct order.
user_code_snippet: count open and close brackets, check if counts match
hint: Equal counts are necessary but not sufficient. The string ({)} has equal counts but is invalid because the closing order is wrong. You need a structure that remembers which bracket was opened most recently.

problem_context: Check if a bracket string is valid: brackets must close in correct order.
user_code_snippet: I know I need order tracking, thinking about stack
hint: You are on the right track. A stack is perfect here because it enforces LIFO order, exactly how brackets must close. Push opening brackets; when you see a closing bracket check if it matches the top of the stack.

problem_context: Check if a bracket string is valid: brackets must close in correct order.
user_code_snippet: stack=[]; push open, pop and match on close; return stack empty
hint: Solid solution. Make sure to handle two edge cases: an empty stack when you encounter a closing bracket (return False immediately), and a non-empty stack at the end (return False if unclosed brackets remain).

problem_context: Check if a bracket string is valid: brackets must close in correct order.
hint: Imagine reading the brackets left to right. When you see an opening bracket, note it somewhere. When you see a closing bracket, the most recently noted opening bracket must match it. What data structure naturally gives you the most recently added item?

problem_context: Check if a bracket string is valid: brackets must close in correct order.
user_code_snippet: count each type of bracket separately
hint: Counting each bracket type separately still misses ordering. Think of a stack: push any open bracket, and when you see a closing bracket verify it matches what was last pushed. The stack's LIFO property enforces the nesting order you need.

problem_context: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
user_code_snippet: for i in range(n): for j in range(i, n): check if s[i:j] has all unique chars
hint: O(n²) or O(n³) substring enumeration is too slow. Instead of restarting for each starting index, think about maintaining a window that slides forward: only expand or shrink its boundaries rather than recomputing from scratch.

problem_context: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
user_code_snippet: sliding window, left and right pointers, set for window chars
hint: Good thinking. For maximum efficiency, use a hashmap of character→last_seen_index instead of a set. When you encounter a duplicate, jump left directly to max(left, last_seen[char]+1) to skip past the duplicate in O(1).

problem_context: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
user_code_snippet: left=0; char_index={}; for right in range(n): if s[right] in char_index and char_index[s[right]]>=left: left=char_index[s[right]]+1; char_index[s[right]]=right; max_len=max(max_len, right-left+1)
hint: This is the optimal O(n) sliding window solution. Make sure your left pointer update uses max(left, ...) to never move backwards. Your solution handles all edge cases correctly.

problem_context: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
hint: Think of a window — a segment of the string. Start with both ends at position 0. Move the right end forward one character at a time. If the new character is already in your window, move the left end forward until it is no longer there. Track the maximum window size seen.

problem_context: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
user_code_snippet: sort the string and count unique consecutive characters
hint: Sorting destroys the substring structure entirely. A substring must be a contiguous segment of the original string. Focus on the original string using two pointers to define a window boundary.

problem_context: Count distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
user_code_snippet: def ways(n): if n<=1: return 1; return ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)
hint: Your recursive logic is correct! But pure recursion recomputes ways(k) for every k multiple times, leading to O(2^n) time. Notice that ways(n) only depends on the two previous values. Can you compute this iteratively bottom-up?

problem_context: Count distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
user_code_snippet: memoize recursive calls with a cache
hint: Memoization is correct and gives O(n) time. An even more space-efficient approach: since each state only needs the previous two values, you can use two variables instead of an array. This gives O(1) space.

problem_context: Count distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
user_code_snippet: a,b=1,1; for _ in range(n-1): a,b=b,a+b; return b
hint: This is the ideal O(n) time O(1) space solution. It is essentially an optimized Fibonacci computation. Your base cases and the rolling update are correct.

problem_context: Count distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
hint: Think about the last step before reaching the top. You either arrived from step n-1 (took 1 step) or from step n-2 (took 2 steps). So the total ways to reach n equals ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). Work this out from the bottom up starting from ways(1)=1 and ways(2)=2.

problem_context: Count distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
user_code_snippet: BFS from step 0 to step n exploring all paths
hint: BFS would work but it explores all paths giving exponential time. The key insight is that you do not need to explore paths — you just need to count them. The count at each step only depends on the two previous steps, not on the full path.

problem_context: Reverse a singly linked list in-place.
user_code_snippet: collect all values in array, reverse array, create new list
hint: Collecting values works but uses O(n) extra space and creates a new list instead of reversing in-place. Try reversing the actual next pointers. You need to change curr.next to point backwards instead of forwards.

problem_context: Reverse a singly linked list in-place.
user_code_snippet: I need prev and curr pointers, must save next before changing curr.next
hint: Exactly right. The three-pointer pattern is: save next_node = curr.next, then set curr.next = prev, then advance prev = curr and curr = next_node. After the loop prev is your new head.

problem_context: Reverse a singly linked list in-place.
user_code_snippet: prev=None; while curr: nxt=curr.next; curr.next=prev; prev=curr; curr=nxt; return prev
hint: This is the O(n) time O(1) space optimal in-place solution. Your pointer manipulation order is correct. Make sure your initial state is prev=None and curr=head.

problem_context: Reverse a singly linked list in-place.
hint: Start with two pointers: prev=None and curr=head. At each step you want to make curr point backward to prev. But if you do curr.next=prev you lose the rest of the list. So first save curr.next in a temp variable, then safely flip the pointer.

problem_context: Find target index in a sorted array in O(log n).
user_code_snippet: for i in range(len(arr)): if arr[i]==target: return i
hint: Linear scan is O(n) which violates the O(log n) requirement. Since the array is sorted, you can eliminate half the remaining candidates at each step. Think about checking the middle element and deciding which half to continue searching.

problem_context: Find target index in a sorted array in O(log n).
user_code_snippet: left and right pointers, compute mid, compare arr[mid] to target
hint: Good. The key detail is the termination condition: use while left <= right (not strict less than) so you consider the case where left and right converge on the same element. Use mid = left + (right-left)//2 to prevent integer overflow in other languages.

problem_context: Find target index in a sorted array in O(log n).
user_code_snippet: left=0; right=n-1; while left<=right: mid=(left+right)//2; if arr[mid]==target: return mid elif arr[mid]<target: left=mid+1 else: right=mid-1; return -1
hint: This is the correct canonical binary search. O(log n) time O(1) space. Make sure your updates are left=mid+1 and right=mid-1 (not mid) to avoid infinite loops when left==right.

problem_context: Find target index in a sorted array in O(log n).
hint: Because the array is sorted, if the middle element is less than target, the target must be in the right half. If greater, it must be in the left half. You can throw away half the array at each step, giving you log n steps total.

problem_context: Merge nums2 into nums1 in-place. nums1 has extra trailing space for nums2 elements.
user_code_snippet: nums1 = nums1 + nums2; nums1.sort()
hint: Concatenating and sorting is O((m+n)log(m+n)) and ignores the fact that both arrays are already sorted. A true merge should be O(m+n). More importantly, you must modify nums1 in-place, not create a new list.

problem_context: Merge nums2 into nums1 in-place. nums1 has extra trailing space for nums2 elements.
user_code_snippet: merging from front overwrites elements, maybe fill from back using extra space
hint: Exactly the key insight. Merging from the back is safe because you write into the trailing empty slots of nums1. Use three pointers: p1 at index m-1, p2 at n-1, and p at m+n-1. Always place the larger element at position p and decrement accordingly.

problem_context: Merge nums2 into nums1 in-place. nums1 has extra trailing space for nums2 elements.
user_code_snippet: p1=m-1; p2=n-1; p=m+n-1; while p2>=0: if p1>=0 and nums1[p1]>nums2[p2]: nums1[p]=nums1[p1]; p1-=1 else: nums1[p]=nums2[p2]; p2-=1; p-=1
hint: This is optimal. One small thing: after the main loop, if p1 becomes -1 but p2 is still >= 0, the else branch already handles copying remaining nums2 elements. Make sure your loop condition is while p2 >= 0 only, since leftover nums1 elements are already in place.

problem_context: Merge nums2 into nums1 in-place. nums1 has extra trailing space for nums2 elements.
hint: Both arrays are sorted, so the largest remaining element is always at the end of one of them. Fill nums1 from the back: compare the last real element of nums1 with the last element of nums2, place the larger one at the very end, and move that pointer left.

problem_context: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.
user_code_snippet: for i in range(n): for j in range(i,n): compute sum(nums[i:j+1]); track max
hint: O(n²) enumeration recomputes sums from scratch each time. There is a linear algorithm: at each position decide whether to extend the current subarray or start a new one. A negative running sum only hurts future elements.

problem_context: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.
user_code_snippet: reset current_sum to 0 when it becomes negative
hint: Almost correct. Reset to the current element (not 0) so your subarray always contains at least one element. This handles all-negative arrays correctly: current_sum = max(num, current_sum + num) at each step.

problem_context: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.
user_code_snippet: curr=nums[0]; best=nums[0]; for num in nums[1:]: curr=max(num, curr+num); best=max(best, curr)
hint: This is Kadane's algorithm, optimal at O(n) time O(1) space. Initializing with nums[0] correctly handles all-negative arrays. Your solution is complete and correct.

problem_context: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.
hint: At each position you face one decision: should I extend my current subarray by including this element, or discard everything before and start fresh here? Starting fresh is better only if the running sum has become negative (it would drag the total down). This leads to a single-pass O(n) solution.

problem_context: Return true if any value appears at least twice in the array.
user_code_snippet: for i in range(n): for j in range(i+1,n): if nums[i]==nums[j]: return True
hint: O(n²) pair comparison works but is slow. You only need to know if you have seen a value before in a single pass. A set gives O(1) average lookup and insertion, reducing this to a single O(n) pass.

problem_context: Return true if any value appears at least twice in the array.
user_code_snippet: sort first then check adjacent elements
hint: Sorting + adjacent check is O(n log n) and correct. But a hash set approach is O(n) and requires only one pass. Both are valid trade-offs: sorting uses O(1) extra space, set uses O(n) but is faster.

problem_context: Return true if any value appears at least twice in the array.
user_code_snippet: seen=set(); for n in nums: if n in seen: return True; seen.add(n); return False
hint: This is the optimal O(n) time O(n) space solution. Early return on first duplicate found is a good optimization. An even more concise version: return len(nums) != len(set(nums)), though your explicit version is clearer for interviews.

problem_context: Return true if any value appears at least twice in the array.
hint: As you walk through the array, keep a running memory of every value you have encountered. For each new element, check if it is already in your memory before adding it. A Python set does both operations in O(1) average time.
